Copper−Iron-Catalyzed Cross-Coupling of ortho-Substituted
Sulfonamides with Sterically Hindered (Hetero)aryl Chlorides and
Alkyl Halides: Synthesis of Sulfonamide Drugs
Keya Roy, Anay Saha, Sampa Mondal, and Laksmikanta Adak*

Cite This: Org. Lett. 2026, 28, 32−38
Read Online

Metrics & More

ABSTRACT: We describe for the first time an effective copper−iron-catalyzed cross-coupling strategy that enables the reaction for
a diverse array of ortho-substituted primary (hetero)aryl and aliphatic sulfonamides with challenging sterically hindered (hetero)aryl
chlorides, bromides, and alkyl halides under solvent-minimized conditions. The developed methodology efficiently affords the
corresponding products, N-aryl, N-heteroaryl, and N-alkyl sulfonamides bearing highly encumbered ortho substituents, in good to
excellent yields with vast substrate scope (104 examples), tolerating several sensitive functionalities. In addition, selective C−N
coupling of substrates containing multiple nucleophilic NH2 groups was effectively accomplished. This economically attractive
protocol was effectively utilized for the synthesis of 10 commercially available sulfonamide-based drugs and 11 drug-like molecules.
Notably, the methodology offers several other important advantages, including gram-scale synthesis, reusability of the catalyst,
synthetic transformations of synthesized cross-coupled products, and elimination of conventional workup. Several spectroscopic
experiments were conducted to identify the oxidation state involved in the active catalytic species. To explore the reaction
mechanistic pathway, a radical clock experiment employing a radical probe and control reactions with radical scavengers were carried
out.

N-Aryl and N-heteroaryl sulfonamides represent a vital class of
compounds with broad applications in medicinal and agricul-
tural chemistry.1 Beyond these areas, sulfonamide derivatives
also play important roles as organocatalysts,2 chiral ligands,3 and
as key building blocks in various chemical transformations.4

Consequently, the development of efficient and versatile
synthetic strategies to construct diverse sulfonamide scaffolds
is of considerable interest, particularly for accessing complex
molecules relevant to drug discovery. However, the synthesis of
structurally intricate sulfonamides, especially those bearing
sterically hindered or heteroaryl substituents, remains a
significant synthetic challenge. In particular, sterically congested
N-aryl sulfonamides and N-heteroaryl sulfonamides are highly
desirable motifs due to their prevalence in biologically active
molecules.5

Traditional methods for synthesizing (hetero)aryl sulfona-
mides typically rely on the condensation of amine nucleophiles
with reactive sulfinyl electrophiles such as arylsulfonyl halides,
esters, azides, or hydrazides to form N−S bonds.6 However,

these approaches often suffer from several drawbacks, including
restricted diversity of substrates, poor tolerance toward
functional groups, harsh reaction conditions, and side reactions.
Moreover, concerns over the potential genotoxicity7 of both
amine nucleophiles and sulfonyl halides have prompted the
development of alternative, safer synthetic strategies. In this
context, C−N coupling reactions between aryl halides and
sulfonamides catalyzed by palladium,8 nickel,9 and copper10 in
combination with ligands have emerged as a promising approach
because of the commercial availability of both coupling partners.

In recent decades, palladium-catalyzed coupling reactions
have been widely employed to facilitate the coupling reaction of
primary sulphonamides with aryl halides, typically in the
presence of bulky phosphine ligands (Scheme 1a).8a−g These

methodologies demonstrate excellent scope for (hetero)aryl
bromides; however, their applicability to (hetero)aryl chlorides
remains limited.8b−i Despite their usefulness, these protocols
face several limitations, including the use of costly palladium
catalysts and specialized ligands. Furthermore, the catalytic
systems often exhibit poor reactivity with sterically hindered or
heteroaromatic coupling partners.8a−d,f−i

Alternatively, cost-effective metals such as nickel with ligand
have been explored for these transformations (Scheme 1a).
These reactions are often conducted in the presence of
expensive phosphine ligands,9a diamine-derived ligands,9b,e−g

or ether-based ligands.9c,d,h While promising, these nickel-
catalyzed methods are largely limited to aryl bromides, iodides,
and a narrow subset of electron-deficient or electronicallyneutral
aryl chlorides.9b,c,e−h Notably, examples involving electron-rich
or sterically hindered (hetero)aryl chlorides remain scarce.

Recent advances in photochemical9b−d,f−h and electro-
chemical9e techniques have further expanded the utility of
nickel catalysis for the formation of the C−N bond, particularly
for reactions in-between aryl bromides and sulfonamides
(Scheme 1a). These approaches often require the use of costly
or toxic ligands, expensive photocatalysts, strong bases, or
reactive alkoxide salts and additives, potentially limiting their
scalability and widespread use.9

Researchers have also explored copper-based catalytic
systems, often paired with electron-rich oxalamides10a or
chelating 1,2-diamine ligands10b−e or polydentate chelating
ligands,10f,g for N-arylation reactions of primary sulfonamides
with aromatic halides. These ligands play a critical role in
stabilizing the copper center and enhancing the catalytic activity
in homogeneous reactions. However, copper-catalyzed methods
have thus far been largely limited to (hetero)aryl iodides and
bromides.10b−g These protocols often rely on high-cost and
complex synthesis of some ligands, which limits their
practicality. Ma and co-workers recently reported a noteworthy
result through the development of a copper(I) oxide (Cu2O)-
catalyzed system using oxalamide ligands for the coupling

reaction of primary sulfonamides with (hetero)aryl bromides
and chlorides (Scheme 1b).10a However, the protocol still faces
several major drawbacks, such as the requirement for costly
electron-rich oxalamide ligands, the use of strongly reactive
alkoxide bases. Moreover, the study did not include aliphatic
halides, sterically hindered (hetero)aryl chlorides, and ortho-
substituted sulfonamides as coupling partners, restricting its
broader applicability. Recently, two reports have described
ligand-free copper-catalyzed cross-coupling reactions of sulfo-
namides with aryl iodides and bromides.11 However, these
methods failed to afford any coupling product when applied to
aryl chlorides or aliphatic reactants, and were also ineffective
with heteroaromatic or sterically hindered coupling partners.

Pd, Ni, and Cu catalytic systems usually require the use of
specific ligands and a strong base, which leads to the problems of
functional group compatibility and low selectivity, particularly
for sulphanilamide (selective C−N coupling with multiple
nucleophilic NH2 groups).8−10 Furthermore, these cross-
coupling methods often fail to couple sterically hindered
(hetero)aryl chlorides with ortho-substituted sulfonamides.
Notably, the coupling of alkyl halides with sulfonamides remains
unexplored using Pd, Ni, or Cu catalysis, despite the importance
of N-alkyl sulfonamides in drug development,5c highlighting a
significant gap in current synthetic methodologies. Thus, the
development of a general, efficient, and sustainable method to
access structurally complex sulfonamides, including drug or
drug-like scaffolds, remains a key goal in synthetic chemistry.

Recent developments in dual transition-metal catalysis have
enabled effective approaches to cross-coupling reactions.12 In
particular, the synergistic combination of iron and copper
catalysts has emerged as a promising strategy, leveraging the
earth-abundance, low toxicity, and complementary reactivity of
both metals, attributes that have shown great potential in cross-
coupling chemistry. Recently, we have developed cost-effective,
environmentally benign, and readily available bimetallic systems
capable of efficiently facilitating C−N bond construction via
cross-coupling between primary amides and aryl halides.13

Herein, we report for the first highly effective copper−iron-
catalyzed cross-coupling reaction of a wide variety of heteroaryl
and aryl chlorides and bromides, as well as alkyl halides, with
diverse primary heteroaryl-, aryl-, and aliphatic sulfonamides
under solvent-minimized conditions without using any exter-
nally added ligand (Scheme 1c). This bimetallic catalytic system
proves particularly effective for the coupling of ortho-substituted
primary sulfonamides with challenging, sterically hindered
(hetero)aryl chlorides and bromides, substrates that have been
notoriously difficult to engage using existing transition-metal
catalysts (Pd, Ni, or Cu). The developed protocol is
economically attractive and delivers the corresponding cross-
coupling product, N-aryl, N-heteroaryl, and N-alkyl sulfona-
mides bearing highly encumbered ortho substituents in good to
excellent yields.

To achieve the optimized reaction conditions, a series of
experiments were conducted for the representative reaction
between benzenesulfonamide and chlorobenzene.14a

To explore the reaction scope, a variety of aryl chlorides and
bromides bearing diverse and challenging substituents, as well as
several challenging sulfonamides, were initially investigated
(Scheme 2). The coupling reaction between benzenesulfona-
mide and both chlorobenzene and bromobenzene afforded the
targeted product 1 in excellent yield under standard reaction
conditions. Subsequently, we focused on exploring the cross-
coupling reaction of sterically hindered partners, which

successfully provided the desired products (2−9) in high
yields.15 The reaction of 2-chloroanisole with benzenesulfona-
mide using a copper catalyst in the presence of a ligand was
previously attempted, but resulted in a trace amount of the
product 3.10a This observation showcases the efficiency of our
established catalytic system toward deactivated aryl chlorides.
We extended our protocol to more challenging conditions by
introducing steric bulk to both coupling partners. We were
pleased to find that our developed methodology performed with
high success in reactions between coupling partners possessing
sterically hindered ortho substituents, yielding the products 10−
20 in high yield, highlighting the exceptional compatibility of
our method with steric challenges. Notably, several aryl
chlorides and bromides bearing substituents at the ortho,
meta, and para positions successfully underwent coupling

reactions with meta- and para-substituted arylsulfonamides as
well as polyaromatic sulfonamides, yielding products 21−27 in
good to excellent yields. It is notable that 1,2-dibromobenzene
and 1,3,5-tribromobenzene underwent selective cross-coupling
with aryl sulfonamides, affording products 7, 14, and 21 in
excellent yields. The retained bromide groups in these products
indicate their suitability for subsequent cross-coupling pro-
cesses, thereby broadening the possibilities for further chemical
modifications.

The coupling reaction was investigated with diverse
heteroaromatic structures for both coupling partners (Scheme
2). (Hetero)aryl chlorides and bromides reacted successfully
with (hetero)arylsulfonamides, providing N-heteroaryl sulfona-
mides 28−34 with 61−83% yield. The protocol was not
restricted to single heteroaromatic coupling partners, as the
optimal reaction condition was efficiently applied for the
coupling reaction of heteroaromatic primary sulfonamides
with heteroaryl chlorides and bromides, providing highly

Scheme 2. Copper−Iron-Catalyzed Cross-Coupling of
(Hetero)aryl or Aliphatic Sulfonamides with (Hetero)aryl or
Alkyl Chlorides and Bromidesa

(heteo)aryl or alkyl halides (0.75 mmol), Fe(acac)3 (5 mol %), CuI
(5 mol %), K2CO3 (0.75 mmol), DMSO (100 μL for 0.5 mmol scale
of reaction) under N2 atmosphere. Isolated yields are reported.

enriched heteroatomic structured secondary sulfonamides 35−
37 with moderate to good yield.
The coupling reactions are not limited to aromatic or
heteroaromatic substrates; they also proceeded effectively with
sterically hindered aliphatic primary sulfonamides and challeng-
ing alkyl chlorides and bromides, as well as styryl bromide, to
produce coupling products 38−46 in high yields (Scheme 2).
These results highlight the wide applicability and robust nature
of this methodology.

Finally, to demonstrate the practicability of this novel
copper−iron-catalyzed method and its potential application
for the synthesis of commercially available drugs and drug-like
molecules, we prepared a range of pharmaceutically established
secondary sulfonamide drugs5a−c,9b,h,10a,16 (Scheme 3).

In this study, it was observed that 4-amino benzenesulfona-
mide underwent a highly selective C−N cross-coupling reaction,
leaving the primary amine group intact. This selectivity toward
C−N coupling in the presence of multiple nucleophilic NH2
groups enabled the efficient synthesis of antibiotic, antimicro-
bial, and antimalarial drug molecules 47−56 with good yields.
Aryl chlorides and bromides, bearing trifluoromethyl and other
sensitive functional groups including nitro, acyl, ester, and vinyl,
are well tolerated, resulting in biologically and medicinally
demanding secondary sulfonamides (57−65) with yields of up
to 89%. Furthermore, our optimal cross-coupling strategy was
effectively employed in the synthesis of Dabrafenib (66), an
anticancer drug, achieving an 81% yield, and Dofetilide (67), an
antiarrhythmic drug, which was obtained in 89% yield. These
results highlight the practical utility of our methodology in
pharmaceutical synthesis.

To showcase the practical utility of the cross-coupling
reaction, a synthesis on a gram scale was conducted under the
optimized reaction conditions, affording the desired secondary
sulfonamide product 13 in a comparable yield within the same
time period relative to the lower millimolar reaction scale.14b

To assess the practical applicability of the protocol, we carried
out several synthetic transformations using our synthesized
cross-coupled products 1,14c 14, 31, and 54. The products 14
and 54 (antimicrobial drug) underwent further cross-coupling
with benzenesulfonamides under the optimized reaction
conditions, affording the extended cross-coupled products 68
and 69 in 62% and 58% yield, respectively (eqs 1 and 2).
Moreover, we employed product 31 in C−H functionalization
reactions where the quinoline moiety acts as a directing group.
Under cobalt catalysis, compound 31 underwent efficient
C(sp2)−H iodination, while palladium catalysis facilitated
C(sp2)−H selenylation, yielding products 70 and 71,
respectively, in 71% and 42% yields (eq 3). The catalyst was
successfully reused for up to five consecutive cycles without
significant loss of catalytic activity.14d

To investigate the mechanism of the cross-coupling reaction,
preliminary mechanistic studies were conducted. As an initial
approach, a radical clock experiment was performed under
standard reaction conditions employing 1-(allyloxy)-2-chlor-
obenzene as a radical probe (eq 4). This experiment yielded the
direct cross-coupling product 72 without generating a ring-
closed cross-coupling product, indicating that radical inter-
mediates are not generated in the reaction. Subsequently, the
reaction was conducted in the presence of a few radical
scavengers, and a noteworthy amount of product 1, was still
isolated, further supporting the conclusion that the reaction
proceeds through a nonradical pathway.14e

A series of experiments were carried out to identify the
oxidation state of the active catalytic species participating in the
mechanistic cycle and to explore the reaction mechanism. X-ray
photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) was utilized to perform the
high-resolution Fe 2p spectrum of the sample.14f This
experiment confirms the presence of Fe(II) and Fe(III)
oxidation states in the reaction mixture.13a,17 Furthermore, the
experiment also suggests that Cu is present in the +1 oxidation
state within the active catalytic species.14g,13a,18

UV spectroscopy was analyzed which supports the presence of
Fe(II), Fe(III), and Cu(I) species in the reaction mixture.14h

Powder X-ray diffraction (PXRD) analysis of the residual
powder, collected after extracting the organic compounds,14i

indicated the existence of both Fe(II) and Fe(III) species, along
with Cu(I).13a,19

Based on mechanistic studies and prior literature re-
ports,10d−f,20 a plausible mechanistic pathway is proposed in
Scheme S2. The proposed reaction mechanism proceeds
through three elementary steps: (i) The aryl halide undergoes
oxidative addition to the catalytically active copper(I) species A,
generating intermediate B.10d−f,20 The sulfonamide substrate or
acetylacetonate (acac) might coordinate with the active catalytic
species, potentially assisting in the oxidative addition process.
(ii) transmetalation of intermediate B with an iron-amide
species to yield intermediate C;21 and (iii) reductive elimination
from intermediate C to produce the cross-coupling product and
to regenerate the involved active copper(I) species A.

In summary, we report the first efficient copper−iron-
catalyzed cross-coupling reaction of sterically hindered
(hetero)aryl chlorides and bromides with ortho-substituted
primary sulfonamides under solvent-minimized conditions and

in the absence of any externally added ligand. This method was
successfully extended to a broad range of aryl, heteroaryl, and
alkyl chlorides and bromides, as well as various primary
heteroaryl-, aryl-, and aliphatic sulfonamides. It demonstrates a
wide scope of substrates with 104 examples and shows excellent
compatibility with various sensitive functional groups, including
−COCH3, −CO2Me, −CO2Et, −CN, −NO2, −NH2, −Br, −Cl,
−F, −CF3, −OCF3, −OCH3, −CH2Ph, vinyl, and heterocycles.
Notably, this approach allows for selective C−N cross-coupling
reaction despite the presence of multiple nucleophilic NH2
groups, preserving the primary amine functionality. Addition-
ally, the method has been effectively utilized in the synthesis of
10 commercially available sulfonamide-based drugs and 11
pharmaceutically important scaffolds, highlighting its signifi-
cance in medicinal chemistry. Several synthetic transformations,
such as further cross-coupling and C−H functionalization, were
performed using our synthesized cross-coupled products. The
protocol is also applied to gram-scale synthesis, demonstrating
its practicality for larger-scale applications. Moreover, this
protocol avoids the need for conventional workup procedures,
enhancing overall efficiency and simplicity. Importantly, the
catalyst employed is environmentally benign, cost-effective, and
demonstrates reusability for at least four reaction cycles. The
reaction mechanism for the cross-coupling was also investigated.
